title: Photography Atlas content follow-up source audit

sample.finding: The capability and limits are supported: PPA explains low angles can enlarge apparent stature and high views can foreshorten (actual lines 59–64); Faulds gives opposite choices for different subject goals (PPA lines 96–104); NAVEDTRA explains height/tilt distortion (lines 18–24). The evidence row points to PPA lines 94–101, which discuss negative space/crop, not angle-of-view. Correct only that locator to lines 59–64. No content downgrade warranted.

sample.risk: high professional_consensus; cosplay-specific transfer and lineage
sample.finding: Both sources directly support Japanese-sword cosplay posing by character type and photographic readability. Nikon Lesson11 explicitly says to adapt stance to character/work, choose period-consistent scene, and use a wooden prop under safety controls; COSPLAY MODE explains character-dependent stances and turns the blade broadside to camera because edge-on it reads as a line. This is Japanese-sword cosplay, not actual weapons training or a universal prop rule. Nikon COSGENIC is labeled as powered by COSPLAY MODE, so publication lineage overlaps; the named authors/practitioners are different, therefore the independence key should encode actual contributors and preserve the overlap note. High is defensible only for this narrow capability, not for a broad weapon-pose consensus.

Aldred’s authored text explicitly distinguishes short-duration high-speed flash from HSS and warns ambient contribution can leave a sharp flash image plus blur; Nikon Kubota describes HSS as rapid pulses during focal-plane shutter travel and power loss; Carpenter explains flash duration freezing when ambient is controlled. Written sources support the exact distinction. Their associated videos were not used. High is defensible for mechanism distinction and choosing by ambient/sync conditions.

Adobe directly states direction/shadow should match and light quality should be similar, including warm/cool and harsh/soft mismatch. PHLEARN provides a full written, named educator demonstration comparing highlight/shadow levels in a single dominant-sky-light composite. That second source supports tonal diagnosis in the stated example, not a universal multi-light rule; current skill does not force that universal interpretation. Two distinct instructional lineages support the capability.

Adobe states use the same point of view and similar scale; PHLEARN says to correct background perspective before other composite correction steps. Both are full-text sources, and the practical skill is limited to comparing/viewpoint matching and avoiding excessive rescue scaling. No source-url or claim mismatch found.

Nikon’s live article recommends deciding what moves, and gives a specific example: keep a flower still for the first 0.5 seconds during a 1-second exposure, then move it. The Society article contrasts a relatively still subject with moving fabric and flash/ambient blur; it says exposure timing and number of takes vary. The “one successful photo” acceptance criterion is a project exercise criterion, not a claim that professionals prescribe a numeric standard. The current wording treats it as acceptance, not consensus, so the distinction is acceptable.

Nikon Ambassador Dave Black directly recommends a stand-in lighting test and correct exposure before an important short portrait slot. Mark Edward Harris separately says to practice in advance and not debut a complex flash effect during an important assignment. Full-text source claims align with the skill. No lesson-video inference or threshold overclaim observed.

Lubezki (ARRI), Edu Grau (ARRI), and Jay Holben (ASC) directly discuss story-motivated camera movement and rehearsal/blocking in cinema. The current skill is explicitly under domain_hint=动态影像 and module moving-image-5; it does not claim static-portrait consensus. Support is appropriate within moving-image cinematography. Do not reuse these film sources to label static portrait camera movement as professional consensus.

source_corrections.recommendation: Replace generic cosplaymode-contributor-line with named author/adviser identities from the page byline (Mame Mayo; adviser Jisai Tatsumura and suit-actor adviser); note that COSGENIC is also powered by COSPLAY MODE. This makes independence transparent; it does not imply the authors are duplicated.

limitations: This is an 8-skill risk-weighted content sample, not a semantic audit of all 247 skills or all 205 sources.
The 17 pages below were opened/reopened; linked example images were not pixel-reviewed unless explicitly stated (none were).
One source-map record, cosplay-cosplaymode-katana, shares a publisher ecosystem with COSGENIC. The page bylines name distinct practitioners; source metadata should make that relationship legible.
One separate exploratory page (Oklahoma State film textbook chapter, used by perspective-skill-height-vs-pitch) returned HTTP 403 in this pass and was excluded from the selected eight.
